source.title: How Abilities in Large Language Models are Affected by Supervised Fine-tuning Data Composition
source.authors: Guanting Dong; Hongyi Yuan; Ke-Ming Lu; Cheng-Peng Li; Mingfeng Xue; Dayiheng Liu; Wei Wang; Zheng Yuan; Chang Zhou; Jing-Ren Zhou

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Some table values appear inconsistent: Table 1 gives the LLaMA-13B code-only HumanEval score as 17.1, while Table 9 gives 18.4 for the single-domain k=1 result.
record.tranche_reason: The study compares downstream benchmark performance across model sizes, providing a different measure of the downstream-scale relationship. It does not measure pretraining loss or fit the original pretraining scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports many SFT data-amount and data-composition results, but these are benchmark scores after SFT, not held-out pretraining loss or tests of a power-law fit. They are not rows for the listed versions. Rows below retain the model-size comparisons relevant to V6.
record.test_reason: This is an SFT data-composition study, not a scaling-law study. It does report post-SFT GSM8K, HumanEval and MT-Bench scores for LLaMA-7B, 13B and 33B at fixed SFT data amounts, and states that larger models generally score higher. That bears on V6 (downstream improvement with model scale) in a new setting: post-SFT, three sizes, no fitted law. It fits T3 better than T2, because the study does not aim at the scaling question.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. Distinct abilities scale differently with SFT data, and larger models generally perform better at the same data amount, except with very little data. Mixing sources helps at low resource and conflicts at high resource, and this low-resource gain grows with model size. Data amount matters more than data ratio. Sequential training causes forgetting, and the proposed DMT strategy mitigates conflicts and forgetting.
record.recipe_differences: The study varies SFT dataset composition, amount, and strategy, then evaluates benchmark abilities; it does not fit pretraining-loss power laws or optimize parameter/token allocation for a compute budget.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported outcomes vary with model size, SFT data amount, ability/domain, and data composition; the paper notes an MT-Bench scoring limitation because it relies on GPT-4.

fits_no_version.finding: Post-SFT benchmark scores scale with SFT data amount in ability-specific ways. Math rises steadily. General ability emerges with about 1k samples and then plateaus. Code is irregular at 7B/13B and roughly log-linear at 33B.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Downstream performance after SFT scales with fine-tuning data amount, with ability-dependent curve shapes.

fits_no_version.finding: The low-resource gain from mixing SFT sources grows with model size for math and general abilities.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Larger models benefit more from mixed-domain SFT data under low-resource conditions.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics, 2023
record.problems: The study does not measure held-out pretraining loss or fit scaling laws. It reports no error bars or uncertainty for the comparisons. The authors note that MT-Bench relies on GPT-4 scoring and may vary or differ from human judgments. Table 1 and Table 9 give inconsistent LLaMA-13B single-domain code HumanEval values.
record.rows_left_out: No additional model-size comparison rows retained. The many SFT data-amount, mixed-domain, training-strategy, and other benchmark results in Figures 2-13 and Tables 1-13 concern post-SFT task scores or SFT data composition, not a listed version's loss scaling law.

untested.parts: Pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute is not measured.
No fitted law and no extrapolation.
Loss power-law form under fine-tuning is not tested. SFT results are benchmark scores without any fitted form.
Predictability from pretraining loss, any fitted predictive law, and more than three model sizes. Model size is also confounded with pretraining tokens (33B used more tokens) and with SFT.

missing.what: Model-size comparisons at intermediate SFT data amounts (k=1/4, 1/16, 1/64). For example, code at k=1/64 is 9.14, 12.20 and 18.59; general at k=1/4 is 5.85, 6.03 and 6.66. Mostly monotone in size.
Model-size comparisons under mixed-domain SFT and under the different training strategies. Code under multi-task learning is non-monotone: 14.63, 19.50, 18.9.

record.verdict_notes: The study cites Kaplan only to estimate SFT FLOPs, which is tool use, not a test. The V6 evidence is thin: three LLaMA sizes, post-SFT, no error bars except MT-Bench averaged over three runs and DMT seeds, and no predictive fit. The Table 1 versus Table 9 discrepancy for 13B code-only (17.1 vs 18.4) is likely a table error.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens, and compute; power-law behavior and bottleneck conditions.
Prediction of much larger runs from power laws fitted on smaller runs.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocation and its trend with compute.
Effects of architecture details such as depth and width at fixed parameter count.
Whether held-out loss follows the same power-law form in fine-tuning or other modalities and training regimes.
The study compares only LLaMA 7B, 13B, and 33B on benchmark scores after SFT; it does not test predictability from pretraining loss, fit a predictive law, or test broad downstream task coverage.
Dependence of pretraining scaling-law exponents or compute-optimal allocations on fitting choices, and bending of those loss curves.

relationships.condition: Single-domain SFT on math (full and 1/256 data), general (full data), and code (1/256 data), LLaMA 7B/13B/33B
relationships.reason: Post-SFT scores rise with model size in each of these conditions (r1, r2, r5, r6, r7, r8, r9, r10). Only three sizes are tested and no law is fitted.
relationships.display_finding: Post-fine-tuning scores increased with size in every specified setting, although only three sizes were tested and no scaling law was fitted.

relationships.condition: Single-domain code SFT at full data (Code Alpaca k=1)
relationships.reason: There is no HumanEval gain from 7B (18.4) to 13B (17.1 or 18.4); the score then rises to 26.82 at 33B (r3, r4). The authors call code scaling irregular at 7B/13B.
relationships.display_finding: HumanEval scored 18.4 at 7B and 17.1 or 18.4 at 13B before rising to 26.82 at 33B.

relationships.condition: Single-domain general SFT at very low data (ShareGPT k=1/256, 336 samples)
relationships.reason: MT-Bench falls with size: 4.00 to 2.95 to 2.3 (r11, r12). This is a narrow, GPT-4-judged condition that the authors flag as an outlier.
relationships.display_finding: With 336 samples, MT-Bench scores fell from 4.00 to 2.95 to 2.3 as size increased, an outlier condition evaluated by GPT-4.
